home.title: Learn About Your Body
home.subtitle: A safe space to learn about menstruation and puberty
home.description: Everyone goes through changes as they grow up. This app helps you understand these changes in a friendly, easy-to-understand way.

boys.title: For Boys
boys.subtitle: Understanding Menstruation
boys.intro: Learning about menstruation helps you understand and support the people in your life.
boys.whyLearnContent: Understanding menstruation helps you be a better friend, brother, and family member. It breaks down barriers and helps everyone feel more comfortable.
boys.whatIsContent: Menstruation, or having a period, is a natural monthly process that happens in the female body. It's a sign that the body is healthy and working normally.
boys.howToHelpContent: Be understanding, don't make jokes about periods, and be supportive if someone needs help or feels unwell.

basics.title: Understanding Menstruation: The Basics
basics.intro: Let's start with the simple facts about menstruation. It's a natural process that happens in healthy bodies.
basics.whatIsText: Menstruation (also called a period) is when blood and tissue from the uterus comes out through the vagina. This happens once a month for most people with female reproductive systems.
basics.whyHappensText: Every month, the body prepares for a possible pregnancy. The uterus creates a soft, cushiony lining. If pregnancy doesn't happen, this lining isn't needed, so the body sheds it. That's a period!
basics.fact3: The menstrual cycle is about 21-35 days long
basics.fact4: It's a sign of a healthy, functioning body
basics.fact5: About half the world's population experiences periods
basics.biologyText: The menstrual cycle is controlled by hormones. These are natural chemicals in the body that send messages. Think of them like the body's text messages telling different parts what to do!

whyMiss.title: Why Girls Might Miss School or Feel Unwell
whyMiss.intro: Understanding why someone might not feel their best during their period helps you be more supportive.
whyMiss.crampsDesc: Muscle contractions in the uterus can cause stomach pain, similar to a muscle cramp during exercise
whyMiss.tirednessDesc: Hormonal changes and losing blood can make someone feel more tired than usual
whyMiss.headachesDesc: Changes in hormone levels can trigger headaches or make someone feel dizzy
whyMiss.moodChangesDesc: Hormones affect emotions, so someone might feel more sensitive, irritable, or sad
whyMiss.backPainDesc: The cramping can extend to the lower back, making it uncomfortable to sit or stand
whyMiss.understandingText: These symptoms aren't an excuse or exaggeration. They're real physical experiences. Some people have mild symptoms, others have severe ones. Being understanding and not making jokes makes a huge difference.

support.title: How to Be a Supportive Friend
support.intro: You can make a real difference by being understanding and helpful. Here's how:
support.do1Desc: If a friend seems tired or uncomfortable, give them space without prying
support.do2Desc: Don't make a big deal out of it. It's a regular part of life for many people
support.do3Desc: If someone needs a sweater or asks you to carry something, help out without questions
support.do4Desc: If a school club or sports team asks you to keep supplies, say yes
support.do5Desc: If you hear someone making period jokes, let them know it's not okay
support.dont1Desc: Period jokes aren't funny. They make people feel embarrassed and ashamed
support.dont2Desc: Don't ask someone if they're on their period. It's private
support.dont3Desc: It's natural biology, like sweating or growing. Don't act disgusted
support.dont4Desc: If someone has an accident, keep it private. Don't tell others
support.scenario1: A classmate seems quieter than usual
support.scenario1Action: Give them space, but let them know you're there if they need anything
support.scenario2: Someone asks to borrow your jacket
support.scenario2Action: Lend it without asking why. They might need it for privacy
support.scenario3: A friend says they can't play sports today
support.scenario3Action: Accept it without pressing for details. Suggest something low-key instead

myths.title: Busting Common Myths
myths.intro: There are many myths about periods that simply aren't true. Let's clear them up!
myths.fact1: Periods are completely natural and healthy. Menstrual blood is just blood and tissue, no different from a nosebleed
myths.myth2: Girls can't swim or exercise during periods
myths.fact2: Most people can do everything they normally do, including swimming, running, and playing sports. Exercise often helps reduce cramps!
myths.myth3: You can tell when someone has their period
myths.fact3: You cannot tell by looking at someone. Period products are designed to be discreet
myths.fact4: Most periods last 3-7 days. The average is about 5 days
myths.myth5: Only girls need to learn about periods
myths.fact5: Everyone benefits from understanding menstruation. It helps build supportive, educated communities
myths.fact6: Periods are a normal part of life. Open conversations help remove shame and stigma
myths.fact7: Period cramps are real and can be quite painful. They're caused by muscle contractions in the uterus
myths.myth8: You lose a lot of blood during a period
myths.fact8: The average period involves only about 2-3 tablespoons of blood. It might look like more because it's mixed with other fluids

quiz.title: Test Your Knowledge
quiz.intro: Let's see what you've learned! Choose the best answer for each question.
quiz.q1b: The body shedding the uterine lining when pregnancy doesn't occur
quiz.q2: How long does a typical period last?
quiz.q3: What's the BEST way to support a friend during their period?
quiz.q3a: Ask them lots of questions about it
quiz.q3b: Tell everyone so they can help
quiz.q3c: Be understanding, patient, and don't make jokes
quiz.q3d: Pretend you don't know anything about periods
quiz.q4b: You can always tell when someone has their period
quiz.q4c: People can't exercise during their period
quiz.q4d: Periods are a natural, healthy process
quiz.q5: What should you do if someone has a period accident at school?
quiz.q5a: Tell all your friends about it
quiz.q5b: Make jokes to lighten the mood
quiz.q5c: Be discreet and offer to help (like lending a jacket)
quiz.excellent: Excellent! You really understand how to be supportive!
quiz.good: Good job! You're on the right track!
quiz.needsWork: Keep learning! Review the sections again.

summary.title: Key Takeaways
summary.point3: Never make jokes or tease about periods
summary.point5: Educate yourself to be a better ally

girls.title: For Girls
girls.subtitle: Your Body, Your Journey
girls.intro: Your body is amazing! Let's learn about the changes happening and how to take care of yourself.
girls.whatToExpectContent: Periods usually start between ages 9-16. Everyone's body is different, and that's perfectly normal!
girls.yourCycleContent: A menstrual cycle is typically 21-35 days. The period itself usually lasts 3-7 days.
girls.takingCareContent: Learn about different period products, managing cramps, and when to talk to a doctor.
girls.feelingGoodContent: Tips for staying comfortable, eating well, and managing your emotions during your period.
girls.empowermentText: Millions of people experience periods every day. It's a natural, healthy part of growing up. You've got this!

understanding.title: Understanding Menstruation
understanding.whatIsText: Menstruation is a natural monthly process where the uterus sheds its lining through the vagina. This happens when pregnancy doesn't occur. It's a sign your body is working properly!
understanding.whyHappensText: Each month, your body prepares for a possible pregnancy by building a cushiony lining in the uterus. If pregnancy doesn't happen, your body doesn't need this lining, so it sheds it. That's your period!
understanding.howLongText: Most periods last 3-7 days, with an average of 5 days. Your cycle (from the start of one period to the start of the next) is usually 21-35 days.
understanding.firstPeriodText: Getting your first period can feel exciting and a little scary. It usually happens between ages 9-16. You might notice brown or red spotting in your underwear. This is completely normal!

bodyChanges.title: Your Changing Body
bodyChanges.subtitle: Learn about the changes happening in your body
bodyChanges.breastsDesc: Your breasts will begin to grow and develop. They may feel tender sometimes. This usually happens before your first period.
bodyChanges.hairDesc: You'll notice hair growing in new places like underarms and pubic area. This is completely normal and natural.
bodyChanges.skinDesc: Your skin might become oilier, and you may get acne. Washing your face regularly and staying hydrated can help.
bodyChanges.heightDesc: You'll grow taller quickly during puberty. You might notice your feet, hands, and arms growing first.
bodyChanges.hipsDesc: Your hips may widen and your body will develop curves. Everyone develops at their own pace.
bodyChanges.emotionsDesc: Hormones can affect your mood. You might feel more emotional or sensitive. This is normal and temporary.

products.title: Period Products Guide
products.intro: There are many options for managing your period. Choose what feels most comfortable for you!
products.padsDesc: Soft, absorbent pads that stick to your underwear. Great for beginners. Change every 4-6 hours.
products.padsHow: How to use: Remove the backing paper and stick to the center of your underwear. Wrap used pads in toilet paper before disposing.
products.clothPadsDesc: Reusable fabric pads that snap onto underwear. Eco-friendly and economical. Wash after each use.
products.clothHow: How to use: Snap onto underwear. After use, rinse in cold water, then wash with regular laundry.
products.tamponsDesc: Small, absorbent tubes inserted into the vagina. Good for swimming and sports. Change every 4-6 hours.
products.tamponsHow: How to use: Insert gently at an angle. If inserted correctly, you shouldn't feel it. Remove by pulling the string.
products.cupsDesc: Reusable silicone cups that collect blood. Can be worn up to 12 hours. Eco-friendly option.
products.cupsHow: How to use: Fold and insert. Empty, rinse, and reinsert every 12 hours or as needed.
products.underwearDesc: Special absorbent underwear. Washable and reusable. Great as backup protection.
products.underwearHow: How to use: Wear like regular underwear. Rinse and wash after use.
products.choosingText: Start with pads if you're new to periods. You can try other options when you feel comfortable. Many people use different products at different times.

painManagement.title: Managing Cramps and Discomfort
painManagement.intro: Period cramps are common, but there are ways to feel better!
painManagement.heatDesc: A heating pad or hot water bottle on your lower belly can really help relax muscles and reduce pain.
painManagement.exerciseDesc: Gentle activities like walking, yoga, or stretching can help reduce cramps and boost your mood.
painManagement.hydrationDesc: Drink plenty of water. It helps reduce bloating and can ease cramps.
painManagement.restDesc: Your body is working hard. Make sure you get enough sleep and rest when you need it.
painManagement.foodDesc: Eat nutritious foods rich in iron and vitamins. Avoid too much salt, sugar, or caffeine.
painManagement.medicineDesc: Over-the-counter pain relievers can help. Always check with an adult before taking any medication.
painManagement.whenToTalk: When to Talk to an Adult
painManagement.severe: Pain is very severe and stops you from daily activities
painManagement.heavy: Very heavy bleeding (soaking through pads in 1-2 hours)
painManagement.irregular: Very irregular cycles after having periods for 2+ years
painManagement.other: Any other concerns or questions you have

tracking.title: Tracking Your Cycle
tracking.intro: Keeping track of your period helps you know when to expect it and understand your body better.
tracking.reason1: Predict when your next period will start
tracking.reason4: Share accurate information with healthcare providers
tracking.method1: Mark the first day of your period on a calendar
tracking.method2: Count the days until your next period starts
tracking.method3: Note any symptoms or changes you experience
tracking.method4: Look for patterns after tracking for a few months
tracking.calendarDesc: Click on the date your period started. Track for a few months to see your pattern.

myths.title: Period Myths vs Facts
myths.intro: Let's bust some common myths and learn the facts!
myths.myth1: You can't swim during your period
myths.fact1: You can absolutely swim! Use a tampon or menstrual cup, and you're good to go.
myths.fact2: Periods are completely natural and nothing to be ashamed of. It's a sign of a healthy body.
myths.myth3: You lose a lot of blood
myths.fact3: Most people lose only 2-3 tablespoons of blood during their entire period.
myths.fact4: Exercise is actually helpful! It can reduce cramps and improve your mood.
myths.fact5: Cycles vary! Anywhere from 21-35 days is normal. Your cycle is unique to you.
myths.myth6: You can't get pregnant during your period
myths.fact6: While unlikely, it's possible. This is why period education is important!
myths.fact7: Virginity is not a physical state. Using tampons doesn't change anything about your body.
myths.myth8: Period blood is different from regular blood
myths.fact8: Period blood is just like any other blood, mixed with tissue and fluids from the uterine lining.

empowermentSection.title: You're Amazing!
empowermentSection.message1: Your body is doing something incredible. Menstruation is a sign of health and strength.
empowermentSection.message2: Millions of people around the world experience periods every day. You're part of a global sisterhood!
empowermentSection.message3: It's okay to have questions, feel confused, or need help. That's what learning is all about.
empowermentSection.message4: Talk to trusted adults - parents, guardians, teachers, or healthcare providers. They're here to help you.
empowermentSection.message5: Remember: periods are natural, normal, and nothing to be embarrassed about!

quickTips.title: Quick Tips
quickTips.tip1: Keep a small kit with pads, wipes, and spare underwear in your bag
quickTips.tip2: Dark-colored clothes can help you feel more confident
quickTips.tip3: Set a reminder on your phone to change products regularly
quickTips.tip4: Keep a jacket or sweater tied around your waist just in case
quickTips.tip5: Tell a trusted friend or teacher so you have support at school

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Got questions? We've got answers!

questions.a1: A period is the monthly shedding of the uterine lining. It's a normal part of the menstrual cycle and usually lasts 3-7 days.
questions.q2: At what age do periods start?
questions.a2: Periods typically start between ages 9-16, with most girls getting their first period around 12-13 years old. Everyone's body is different!
questions.q3: Is it normal to have irregular periods?
questions.a3: Yes! Especially in the first few years. It can take 2-3 years for your cycle to become regular.
questions.a4: There are many options including pads, tampons, menstrual cups, and period underwear. You can choose what feels most comfortable for you.
questions.q5: Why do I feel emotional during my period?
questions.a5: Hormonal changes during your cycle can affect your mood. It's completely normal to feel more emotional. Self-care and rest can help!
questions.q6: Can I exercise during my period?
questions.a6: Absolutely! Exercise can actually help reduce cramps and improve your mood. Listen to your body and do what feels comfortable.
questions.a7: Mild to moderate cramping is normal. If pain is severe or interferes with daily activities, talk to a doctor or trusted adult.
questions.a8: Typically, people with female reproductive systems get periods. However, some transgender men may also experience periods.

parents.title: Guide for Parents
parents.subtitle: Supporting Your Child Through Puberty
parents.intro: As a parent, you play a crucial role in helping your child understand and navigate puberty.
parents.startConversationContent: Begin conversations early, before puberty starts. Use correct terminology and answer questions honestly.
parents.createSafeContent: Let your child know they can come to you with questions. Avoid showing embarrassment and normalize these discussions.
parents.resourcesContent: Books, websites, and healthcare providers can support your conversations.
parents.prepareKitContent: Help your daughter prepare a small kit with pads, clean underwear, and pain relief for school or activities.
